posts.title: Vienna in Winter
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

Vienna in February is empty in the way a city is only empty when the tourists have decided it is the wrong month. They are wrong.

How the eight days went

The plan was one district a day and one museum every other day, which lasted until the first Kaffeehaus and then became one district a day and as much sitting down as possible.

Everything in this trip is walkable or on the U-Bahn. I did not take a taxi once, and the only thing I booked in advance was the opera.

  • Buy the 72-hour transit pass on day one
  • Museums are quiet before eleven and after four
  • Nothing worth eating is on the Graben
A city you can cross on foot in an hour is a city you will actually see.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: Eight days, one city, and the coldest good coffee in Europe.

posts.title: Austria by Rail
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

Austria is the rare country where the train is not the compromise. It is the good option, and the car is the compromise.

The route

Vienna to Salzburg, Salzburg to Hallstatt, Hallstatt back through the lakes. Six days, one pass, no timetable anxiety, because there is always another train.

The only part worth planning is Hallstatt, and the only planning it needs is arriving before the coaches.

  • Reserve nothing except the Vienna\u2013Salzburg leg
  • The lake ferry meets the train, not the other way round
  • Rain is not a reason to reschedule anything here
A mountain looks better from a seat you did not have to drive.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: Salzburg, Hallstatt and the lakes — on a rail pass, no rental car.

posts.title: Three Capitals
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

Three capitals that were one empire, close enough that you can eat breakfast in one and dinner in another, and different enough that you would never confuse them.

Ten days, three cities

Four nights in Vienna, three in Prague, three in Budapest, and both train legs in daylight because the countryside between them is the fourth thing worth seeing.

If you only have a week, drop Prague. It is the one that suffers most from being rushed.

  • Vienna \u2192 Prague is four hours; Prague \u2192 Budapest is seven
  • Book the Railjet, not the cheap bus
  • Budapest last, so the baths are the reward
Ten days is enough for three cities and not enough for two of them.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: Vienna, Prague and Budapest in ten days, entirely by train.

posts.title: Goa, Off Season
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

Everyone goes in December. The rain is the point of July, and so is paying a third of the price for the same room.

What is open and what is not

The beach shacks come down before the monsoon and go back up in October, so eating is inland, which is where it should have been anyway.

Swimming is a bad idea for six weeks of this. Everything else about the place improves.

  • Book north Goa, travel south for the day
  • A scooter in the rain is a decision, not a plan
  • The best fish thali is never on the beach
Off season is just the season with fewer people in it.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: The monsoon coast, when the shacks are shut and the rates are honest.

posts.title: The Ringstrasse in one morning
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

The Ringstrasse is a circle of the nineteenth century's best arguments about what a city should look like, and you can see all of it from a two-euro tram seat.

Doing it properly

Take tram 1 clockwise and tram 2 back. That is the whole tour, and it costs less than a coffee.

Get off at the Rathaus, walk two blocks in, and the crowds vanish immediately.

  • Tram 1 and 2 together close the loop
  • The Opera end is the busy end \u2014 start at the other one
  • Everything on the Ring is free from the outside
The best view of a building is usually from the seat of something moving slowly.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: One boulevard, nine buildings, and why the tram beats the walking tour.

posts.title: Kaffeehaus rules nobody tells you
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

A Viennese coffee house sells you a chair for as long as you want it, and the coffee is the rent. Nobody will rush you and nobody will fuss over you either.

The unwritten part

Order a Melange and a glass of water arrives with it. That is not an upsell, it is the format.

Reading a newspaper alone for two hours is the intended use, not an eccentricity.

  • Never ask for the wifi password first
  • Cash is still faster than card in the old ones
  • The waiter is not rude, he is finished talking
The coffee is the rent on the chair, and the chair is the point.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: You are buying the table, not the coffee. Act accordingly.

posts.title: Schönbrunn before the tour buses
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

The palace opens at eight and the gardens open at half past six, which is a ninety-minute head start most people never use.

The order that works

Gardens first in the dark, Gloriette at sunrise, palace at opening, and out before the first coach arrives at ten.

In winter the fountains are off and the hedges are bare, and it looks better for it \u2014 you can see the shape of the thing.

  • Gardens are free; only the palace is ticketed
  • The Gloriette caf\u00e9 opens later than the hill does
  • Skip the Grand Tour if you are short on time
Arriving early is the cheapest upgrade in travel.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: The gardens open at half six and are yours until nine.

posts.title: Naschmarkt on a Saturday
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

The first two hundred metres of the Naschmarkt sell dried fruit at three times the price. Keep walking and it turns into a market.

Where it gets good

Past the restaurants the stalls stop calling out to you, which is the reliable sign you have reached the part locals use.

Saturday adds the flea market at the far end, which is where the trip's only souvenir came from.

  • Go hungry, buy at the far end
  • The flea market is Saturday only
  • Cash, always
Any market's real half starts where the sales patter stops.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: Half of it is for tourists. The other half is worth the trip.

posts.title: Salzburg in the rain is the correct Salzburg
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

It rained for two of the three days and the town lost nothing. The old town is narrow, arcaded and mostly covered, and the fortress is better under cloud.

The day that worked

Fortress first thing on the funicular, down through the old town for lunch, and the Mirabell gardens when the light gives up.

The Mozart houses are a queue in July and an empty room in September.

  • The funicular is included in the fortress ticket
  • Getreidegasse is covered end to end
  • Cross the river for anywhere worth eating
Weather only ruins a place you were going to photograph and not look at.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: The old town is small, covered and better wet.

posts.title: Hallstatt at seven in the morning
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

Hallstatt gets more day visitors than it has beds. Before nine it is a working village on a lake; by eleven it is a queue with a view.

Beating the coaches

Stay the night. That is the whole trick, and there is no second one. The first coach parks at about half nine.

The salt mine funicular opens later than the village does, so do the lake first and the mountain after.

  • Sleep in Obertraun if Hallstatt is full
  • The ferry meets the train from Salzburg
  • The classic photo spot is signposted; the better one is not
You cannot photograph your way out of arriving at the same time as everyone else.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: Two hours of it to yourself, then four thousand people arrive.

posts.title: What an ÖBB rail pass actually costs
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

Every rail pass article quotes the pass. Nobody quotes the reservations, the night you missed the cheap fare, or the bit where a point-to-point ticket would have been cheaper.

The real total

Six days of travel came to less than two days of car hire once fuel and the Vignette were counted, and I did not park anything.

Buy the pass only if you are moving more than every other day. Below that, single tickets win.

  • Reservations are separate and cheap
  • Sparschiene fares beat the pass on single long legs
  • Regional trains need no reservation at all
A pass is a bet that you will keep moving. Make sure you will.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: The numbers, with the reservations nobody includes.

posts.title: Vienna to Prague by train, seat by seat
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

Four hours from centre to centre, no airport, no bag drop, and a window the whole way. The only decision is which side of the carriage.

The seat

Sit on the left going north. The river runs with you for the last hour and the villages are on that side.

The dining car is real and the goulash is better than it needs to be.

  • Book the Railjet, not the bus
  • Left side going north, right side coming back
  • The border is a sign and nothing else
The best hours of a trip are often the ones between the places.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: Four hours, one border you will not notice, and which side to sit on.

posts.title: Prague is two cities and one is for you
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

There is the Prague of the Charles Bridge at noon, and there is the Prague four streets away. They share a postcode and nothing else.

Getting to the second one

Cross the bridge before seven in the morning or after ten at night. In between it is a corridor of people photographing each other.

Vinohrady and Karl\u00edn are where the city carries on while the old town does its job.

  • Old Town Square is a ten-minute visit, not an afternoon
  • The castle is best entered from the top, downhill
  • Anywhere with a menu in six languages is not for you
Every famous view has a time of day when it is still yours.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: Cross the bridge at six or do not cross it at all.

posts.title: Budapest baths, ranked by queue
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

All four are worth it and only one is worth it at midday. The ranking below is by how long you will stand outside, not by how good the water is.

The ranking

Luk\u00e1cs has locals and no queue. Rudas has the roof pool and a booking system. Gell\u00e9rt has the tiles. Sz\u00e9chenyi has the photographs and the wait.

Go at opening or two hours before closing. The middle of the day is a line.

  • Bring your own towel or pay twice for one
  • Rudas rooftop is timed \u2014 book it
  • Sz\u00e9chenyi is best in the rain, in winter
The queue is the price, and it is negotiable by clock.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: Széchenyi, Gellért, Rudas and Lukács — and when to turn up.

posts.title: Goa in the monsoon
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

The rain arrives in sheets for an hour and then stops, and in between the whole coast is green in a way December never shows you.

What it is actually like

The shacks are gone, the sea is closed for swimming, and the inland roads are the best they will look all year.

Rooms cost a third of the December rate and nobody asks for a minimum stay.

  • Check the flag before you swim \u2014 then do not swim
  • Inland Goa is the reason to come now
  • Everything shuts by nine
The off season is not a worse version of the place. It is a different one.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
posts.custom_excerpt: Green, empty, and closed in exactly the places you expected.

posts.title: What a month in Goa costs
posts.mobiledoc:
{"version": "0.3.1", "atoms": [], "cards": [["html", {"html": "

Four weeks, one scooter, one room, and a spreadsheet I kept honestly, including the two days I ate badly and paid for it.

The line items

Rent is the whole budget in December and a rounding error in July. Food barely moves either way.

The costs nobody lists are laundry, the scooter deposit, and the day the wifi fails and you buy a data pack.

  • Monthly rent beats weekly by half
  • Petrol is the cheapest line on the sheet
  • Budget for one wasted day a week in the rain
A budget is only honest if it includes the days that went wrong.
"}]], "markups": [], "sections": [[10, 0], [1, "p", []]]}
